Paid-up Capital & Blocked Account Regime No Capital Lockup Account Required

Paid-in capital rule: SL requires minimum share capital of €3,000 (approx. USD 3,300), fully subscribed and paid in cash or non-cash contributions; a bank certificate confirming payment is required, no escrow account is required because the full amount must be paid at the time of subscription.

Stage 03

Tax Identity & Indirect Tax

Tax authority e-portal, entity tax classification elections, VAT thresholds, and 0% export documentation chain.

Tax ID Application Infrastructure

Competent tax authority

Agencia Estatal de Administración Tributaria (AEAT) — State Tax Administration Agency of Spain; official electronic portal: Sede Electrónica de la AEAT at sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es; customs administration for exports and special taxes is exercised by the Departamento de Aduanas e Impuestos Especiales of AEAT.

E-government filing portal

To obtain the statutory NIF (Número de Identificación Fiscal) for a Spanish Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada (SL) dedicated to dangerous-goods forwarding: (1) acquire a Certificación Negativa de Denominación Social (negative name certificate) from the Registro Mercantil Central; (2) execute the public incorporation deed (Escritura de Constitución) before a Spanish notary; (3) inscribe the deed at the relevant Provincial Mercantile Registry; (4) file Form 036 (Censo de Empresarios, Profesionales y Retenedores) with AEAT to obtain the provisional corporate NIF; and (5) after definitive registry inscription, resubmit Form 036 to activate the conclusive NIF (format: letter plus 7 digits plus control character). The SL is simultaneously enrolled for Corporate Income Tax (Modelo 200 under Ley 27/2014), VAT (Modelo 390 annual return under Ley 37/1992), and, where staff are engaged, employer and withholding registrations; the ISIC 5229 activity and the special 'dangerous goods operator' licence declaration are recorded in the census (IAE classification). A non-resident foreign parent may lawfully hold 100% of the SL subject to no local counterpart requirement. A non-resident entity not having a permanent establishment must separately obtain an NIF/NIE via Form 030 (or Form 036 through a fiscal representative), file Non-Resident Income Tax (IRNR) on Modelo 216, and may be required to appoint a fiscal representative for IRNR and customs procedures.

Tax ID type & application path: Entity_Level_Taxation — To obtain the statutory NIF (Número de Identificación Fiscal) for a Spanish Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada (SL) dedicated to dangerous-goods forwarding: (1) acquire a Certificación Negativa de Denominación Social (negative name certificate) from the Registro Mercantil Central; (2) execute the public incorporation deed (Escritura de Constitución) before a Spanish notary; (3) inscribe the deed at the relevant Provincial Mercantile Registry; (4) file Form 036 (Censo de Empresarios, Profesionales y Retenedores) with AEAT to obtain the provisional corporate NIF; and (5) after definitive registry inscription, resubmit Form 036 to activate the conclusive NIF (format: letter plus 7 digits plus control character). The SL is simultaneously enrolled for Corporate Income Tax (Modelo 200 under Ley 27/2014), VAT (Modelo 390 annual return under Ley 37/1992), and, where staff are engaged, employer and withholding registrations; the ISIC 5229 activity and the special 'dangerous goods operator' licence declaration are recorded in the census (IAE classification). A non-resident foreign parent may lawfully hold 100% of the SL subject to no local counterpart requirement. A non-resident entity not having a permanent establishment must separately obtain an NIF/NIE via Form 030 (or Form 036 through a fiscal representative), file Non-Resident Income Tax (IRNR) on Modelo 216, and may be required to appoint a fiscal representative for IRNR and customs procedures.

Default Tax Classification & Elections

Default tax classification

Entity_Level_Taxation

Available election forms

The SL is a per-se corporate taxpayer; Spain does not provide any US-style 'check-the-box' pass-through election. Available statutory elections include: (a) Group VAT registration (Régimen Especial del Grupo de Entidades) under arts. 126 et seq. LIVA, electable for Spanish-resident related entities meeting 50% voting control and board-appointment rights; (b) Corporate Income Tax consolidation (Régimen de Consolidación Fiscal) under arts. 56-100 LIS, requiring at least 70% direct or indirect ownership (75% where the parent is listed) of Spanish-resident entities and a formal application; (c) the participation exemption and ETVE holdings regimes under art. 21 LIS for foreign-sourced dividends and capital gains; (d) hybrid mismatch and reverse-hybrid transparent-entity rules transposing ATAD (Directive 2016/1164) and ATAD 2 (Directive 2017/952); (e) the reduced 15% CIT regime for newly-created entities on the first EUR 300,000 of taxable base (art. 29.3 LIS); and (f) customs facilitation statuses such as Authorized Economic Operator (AEO) and 'exportador autorizado' (approved exporter). Pass-through treatment cannot be elected post-incorporation for the SL; shareholder-level taxation is confined to dividend and participation exemption rather than flow-through of profits.

VAT / GST & 0% Export Zero-Rating

Mandatory registration threshold (Nexus)

Stage 04

Banking & Treasury Architecture

Central-bank FX diagnosis, tier-1 local banks vs offshore digital EMI matrix, and KYC rejection defense guide.

Foreign Exchange Regime & Central Bank Policy

Current-account convertibility

Spain uses the euro and has no general exchange controls. Current-account payments, including imports, exports, freight services, insurance, salaries, dividends, interest and other ordinary commercial remittances, are generally freely convertible and transferable within the applicable banking, sanctions, tax and anti-money-laundering framework. Capital-account movements are also generally liberalized, but foreign direct investment, certain investments involving non-EU or non-EFTA investors, regulated sectors, sanctioned jurisdictions and transactions subject to national-security screening may require prior authorization, notification or post-investment reporting. An SL may normally remit dividends, loan principal, interest and liquidation proceeds to non-residents after satisfaction of corporate-law, accounting, withholding-tax, transfer-pricing, solvency and beneficial-ownership requirements. Banks may require audited or management accounts, shareholder resolutions, tax-clearance evidence, dividend declarations, loan agreements, proof of source of funds and evidence that the payment is commercially justified. Dividend distributions require distributable profits and must not impair legally required reserves or the company's net-equity requirements. Payments may be delayed or rejected where the bank cannot verify the counterparty, beneficial owner, transaction purpose, dangerous-goods activity, sanctions exposure or underlying documentation.

Export proceeds surrender rules

Spain has no general statutory requirement for an exporter to surrender export proceeds to Banco de España and no general mandatory conversion ratio or universal conversion deadline. Export receipts may generally remain in euros or another permitted currency in an account with a Spanish, EU or other appropriately regulated institution, subject to bank controls, tax records, accounting treatment, sanctions screening and applicable statistical declarations. The company should retain contracts, invoices, transport documents, customs records, bills of lading or air waybills, proof of delivery and bank confirmations. Cross-border payments and balances may be reportable for Banco de España balance-of-payments or external-position statistics when requested or when applicable thresholds and reporting frameworks are met. Cash or bearer negotiable instruments physically entering or leaving the EU at or above EUR 10,000 require the applicable customs declaration; intra-EU movements may also be subject to Spanish cash-control declaration rules. No conversion deadline applies solely because an export invoice has been collected.

Central bank supervision: Banco de España, operating within the Eurosystem under the monetary authority of the European Central Bank. Foreign-exchange restrictions are principally governed by European Union law, Spanish foreign-investment and anti-money-laundering legislation, and Banco de España statistical-reporting rules.

Offshore Digital Bank / EMI Whitelist

Cross-border EMI / Fintech rails Fit: High

Medium for low-complexity euro collections and payments; low to medium for a dangerous-goods freight-forwarding business requiring documentary trade finance, multi-currency settlement, credit facilities or high-value international wires. An offshore digital EMI may lawfully provide services in Spain only if authorized under its home EEA framework and validly passported, or otherwise operating through an appropriate Spanish authorization or agent structure. The provider must be an authorized electronic-money institution or payment institution, must safeguard client funds, and cannot provide bank deposits or ordinary bank credit unless separately licensed. Payment accounts do not provide deposit-guarantee protection equivalent to bank deposits. The EMI may impose enhanced due diligence, transaction limits, prohibited-country rules, source-of-funds reviews and restrictions on hazardous-material counterparties. Use of an EMI does not remove Spanish tax, accounting, sanctions, customs, AML, beneficial-ownership or foreign-payment reporting obligations.

Core KYC Rejection Triggers & Defense Dossier

Business classified as high-risk because it forwards, brokers or arranges transport of regulated hazardous chemicals, explosives, toxic substances, radioactive materials or other dangerous goods.

Root cause: Business classified as high-risk because it forwards, brokers or arranges transport of regulated hazardous chemicals, explosives, toxic substances, radioactive materials or other dangerous goods.

Defense evidence: Company description identifying the precise role as freight forwarder rather than owner, manufacturer or unlicensed carrier; applicable ADR, IMDG Code and IATA Dangerous Goods compliance evidence; transport, customs and safety-management procedures; licenses, permits and registrations of the company and contracted carriers; named dangerous-goods safety adviser where required; staff training records; insurance certificates; customer and route risk-assessment policy; sanctions-screening procedure; and sample redacted shipment files.
Opaque ownership, non-resident shareholders, nominee arrangements, trusts or an inability to verify the ultimate beneficial owner.

Root cause: Opaque ownership, non-resident shareholders, nominee arrangements, trusts or an inability to verify the ultimate beneficial owner.

Defense evidence: Current Spanish commercial-register extract; articles of association; shareholder register; complete ownership chart to natural persons; passports and proof of address for all relevant owners and directors; beneficial-owner declaration; notarized powers of attorney; tax identification numbers; and independent corporate-register extracts for foreign entities.
High-risk jurisdictions, sanctioned counterparties, dual-use chemicals, military end users or unusual trade routes.

Root cause: High-risk jurisdictions, sanctioned counterparties, dual-use chemicals, military end users or unusual trade routes.

Defense evidence: Counterparty master file; end-user and end-use certificates; export-control classification; customs declarations; licenses under EU dual-use and sanctions regimes where relevant; screening results against EU, UN, UK and US lists as contractually required; route and vessel or aircraft details; denied-party escalation records; and documented approval by the compliance officer.
Large or irregular incoming capital, shareholder loans, pass-through funds or payments inconsistent with the declared forwarding activity.

Root cause: Large or irregular incoming capital, shareholder loans, pass-through funds or payments inconsistent with the declared forwarding activity.

Defense evidence: Executed shareholder-loan or capital-contribution agreement; board and shareholder resolutions; bank statements; audited or management accounts; source-of-wealth and source-of-funds evidence; tax filings; financing term sheet; proof of beneficial ownership of the funding party; explanation of expected use; and reconciliation from receipt through operating expenditure.
Multiple unrelated third-party payers, cash-intensive activity, payment-on-behalf-of arrangements or rapid onward transfers.

Root cause: Multiple unrelated third-party payers, cash-intensive activity, payment-on-behalf-of arrangements or rapid onward transfers.

Defense evidence: Written customer-payment policy; agency and freight-forwarding contracts; invoices and shipment references; three-way reconciliation of payer, customer and consignee; segregation-of-funds procedures; transaction-monitoring rules; prohibition on anonymous cash; customer authorization for third-party settlement; and management approval for exceptions.
Insufficient evidence supporting cross-border trade payments or a mismatch between invoice, customs, transport and bank data.

Root cause: Insufficient evidence supporting cross-border trade payments or a mismatch between invoice, customs, transport and bank data.

Defense evidence: Commercial invoice; purchase or service contract; packing list; safety data sheet; export or import declaration; bill of lading, CMR or air waybill; certificate of origin where relevant; freight calculation; proof of delivery; insurance documents; payment instruction; and a transaction-level reconciliation file.
Adverse media, criminal allegations, corruption exposure, politically exposed persons or sanctions-sensitive intermediaries.

Root cause: Adverse media, criminal allegations, corruption exposure, politically exposed persons or sanctions-sensitive intermediaries.

Defense evidence: Independent adverse-media review; PEP and sanctions-screening record; compliance questionnaire; anti-bribery and corruption policy; intermediary due-diligence report; litigation and enforcement disclosure; beneficial-owner explanation; remediation evidence; and senior-management risk acceptance where permitted.
Non-Spanish documents, expired corporate records, inconsistent translations or inability to authenticate foreign signatures.

Root cause: Non-Spanish documents, expired corporate records, inconsistent translations or inability to authenticate foreign signatures.

Defense evidence: Recent apostilled or legalized certificates; sworn Spanish translations where requested; certified copies; electronic verification links; incumbency and good-standing certificates; specimen signatures; and a document-control schedule showing issue dates and renewal dates.

Cross-Border Clearing Corridors & Settlement Fit

Use a regulated Spanish or EEA bank account in the SL's legal name. For share capital, transfer funds from the shareholder's verified account with a payment reference identifying the shareholder, the SL, the capital contribution and the corporate purpose; obtain the bank certificate required for incorporation or the notarial file, then record the contribution in the accounting and commercial-register documentation. For shareholder loans, use a signed loan agreement stating principal, currency, maturity, interest, repayment terms, arm's-length pricing, related-party status and use of proceeds. Maintain a complete source-of-funds and source-of-wealth file. Banks may request the corporate deed, NIF, registry extract, ownership chart, board resolutions, loan or subscription agreement, tax residency certificates and evidence of the remitter's account ownership. There is no general Spanish FX purpose-code regime equivalent to systems used in some controlled-currency jurisdictions; the bank should use accurate SEPA or SWIFT remittance information and any applicable ISO 20022 or correspondent-bank purpose field. Record the transaction as equity, shareholder loan, intercompany service payment or other legally accurate category, never as a generic unexplained transfer. Review foreign-investment notification or authorization requirements, including national-security screening, before or after investment where applicable. Reconcile all receipts to the general ledger and retain records for AML, tax, transfer-pricing, audit and Banco de España statistical-reporting purposes.For ordinary euro payments, use SEPA Credit Transfer through the Spanish bank, with complete payer, payee, IBAN, BIC where required, invoice number, shipment reference and compliance information. For non-SEPA or non-euro payments, use SWIFT customer credit transfer, commonly represented by MT103 in legacy messaging or the corresponding ISO 20022 message, with accurate ordering-customer, beneficiary, intermediary-bank, purpose and regulatory information. For documentary trade, use an irrevocable commercial letter of credit issued or advised through a regulated bank under UCP 600, with confirmation where country or bank risk warrants it; use documentary collections under URC 522 where appropriate. Specify Incoterms, transport document requirements, partial-shipment and transshipment terms, insurance, expiry, presentation period, sanctions clauses and dangerous-goods documentation. Banks will screen all parties, vessels, aircraft, routes, ports, goods descriptions and documents. Do not use vague descriptions such as 'chemicals' where a precise lawful goods description is available. For freight forwarding, retain the underlying customer invoice, carrier invoice, customs record, transport document, safety documentation and proof of service. Outbound dividends, interest and loan repayments require corporate approvals, tax analysis, withholding-tax processing, treaty documentation and arm's-length support. Cash payments should be avoided and must comply with Spanish cash-payment restrictions and declaration rules.Deliverable foreign-exchange forwards with an authorized bank or investment firm, supported by a documented underlying exposure, treasury policy, confirmation, maturity, settlement instructions and accounting designation.Non-deliverable forwards for currencies or corridors where physical delivery is restricted or operationally impractical, subject to counterparty authorization, EMIR requirements, MiFID II classification and appropriateness or suitability procedures where applicable. NDFs do not bypass sanctions, payment restrictions or local-currency controls.Cross-currency swaps and foreign-exchange swaps for documented funding, receivable or payable exposures, subject to counterparty credit limits, collateral terms, valuation, EMIR reporting, netting documentation and board-approved risk limits.Currency options, collars and structured hedges may be used only after assessment of suitability, premium, leverage, downside exposure, accounting treatment and early-termination rights. Complex products should be restricted to appropriately classified professional clients and approved counterparties.Hedges should be matched to forecast or contracted exposures, recorded under a written treasury policy, monitored for effectiveness, and executed only with regulated counterparties under appropriate master documentation such as ISDA and collateral support arrangements where relevant.

E-commerce / gateway settlement fit: Medium for low-complexity euro collections and payments; low to medium for a dangerous-goods freight-forwarding business requiring documentary trade finance, multi-currency settlement, credit facilities or high-value international wires. An offshore digital EMI may lawfully provide services in Spain only if authorized under its home EEA framework and validly passported, or otherwise operating through an appropriate Spanish authorization or agent structure. The provider must be an authorized electronic-money institution or payment institution, must safeguard client funds, and cannot provide bank deposits or ordinary bank credit unless separately licensed. Payment accounts do not provide deposit-guarantee protection equivalent to bank deposits. The EMI may impose enhanced due diligence, transaction limits, prohibited-country rules, source-of-funds reviews and restrictions on hazardous-material counterparties. Use of an EMI does not remove Spanish tax, accounting, sanctions, customs, AML, beneficial-ownership or foreign-payment reporting obligations.

Stage 06

Corporate Tax & Transfer Pricing

Corporate income tax (CIT), box-by-box return breakdown, dividend WHT, and director personal liability.

Statutory corporate income tax (CIT)

25%

Dividend withholding tax (WHT)

19% under Spanish Non-Resident Income Tax (IRNR) on dividends distributed by an SL to non-resident shareholders. EU/EEA corporate shareholders may qualify for a 0% rate under the Parent-Subsidiary Directive where the parent holds at least 5% of the subsidiary's capital and the shareholding has not been held less than one year.

Mandatory Return Breakdown

Deadline: · Frequency:

Filing and payment within 25 days after the six-month anniversary of the tax year end. For a calendar year ending 31 December, the deadline is 25 July of the following year.

Deadline: · Frequency:

Same filing window as Modelo 200: within 25 days after the six-month anniversary of the tax year end; for a 31 December year-end, by 25 July.

Transfer Pricing & Economic Substance

Master / Local File threshold: Local File and Master File become mandatory when the Spanish SL's net turnover (importe neto de la cifra de negocios) exceeds €10,000,000. Below that threshold, simplified documentation is required for related-party transactions exceeding €250,000 per counterparty and for related-party real-estate transactions exceeding €6,000,000. The Master File is also required at the local level when the consolidated group revenue equals or exceeds €10,000,000 under Spanish documentation rules.

Economic substance scope: Spain does not maintain a standalone Economic Substance Regulations (ESR) regime analogous to offshore financial centres, but economic substance is embedded throughout Spanish tax law: (i) an SL has legal residence where management and control are effectively located; (ii) treaty benefits are denied to entities without genuine business purpose under the OECD MLI/limitation-on-benefits concept; and (iii) ATAD and the General Tax Law anti-abuse clause recharacterise artificial arrangements. A dangerous-goods-forwarding SL that functions merely as a letterbox, with no local personnel, premises, commercial decision-making, or physical handling of regulated goods, may be reassessed, denied treaty relief, and subject to criminal tax fraud charges.

Fatal Compliance Red Lines & Director Liability

Tax Evasion and Fraudulent Filing

Statutory sanction: Civil penalty of 50%-150% of the evaded tax plus late interest. If the amount evaded exceeds €120,000, criminal conviction under Article 305 of the Spanish Penal Code carries imprisonment of 1-6 years and a fine of up to six times the defrauded amount.

Director personal liability: Directors may be jointly and severally liable for the corporate tax debt under Article 43.1(b) LGT when they caused or ratified the fraud. Criminal penalties may include personal fines, travel bans, civil restitution, seizure of personal assets, and disqualification from corporate management.
Shell-Company (Letterbox) Abuse

Statutory sanction: Tax reassessment with inclusion of the full economic income plus 25% CIT and penalties up to 150% of unpaid tax. The European anti-abuse rules and Spanish GAAR may deny treaty benefits and disallow the entire artificial structure.

Director personal liability: Directors who sign agreements or tax returns for the letterbox entity are exposed to civil restitution, disqualification, travel bans, and criminal prosecution for tax fraud or money laundering where the sham structure is used to move illegal proceeds.
Transfer Pricing Documentation Failure

Statutory sanction: A transfer pricing adjustment is made under the arm's-length principle, with a 15% penalty on the adjusted amount under Article 114 LIS. Independent documentation penalties under Article 213 LGT range from €1,000 to €15,000 per transaction or deficiency.

Director personal liability: Spanish courts have held directors personally liable when they knowingly approve transfer pricing reports lacking economic substance, do not retain contemporaneous documentation, or otherwise cause the company to fail in its TP obligations; liability includes the resulting tax and penalty amounts.
Anti-Money-Laundering and Dangerous-Goods Compliance

Statutory sanction: Fines under Spanish Law 10/2010 reach up to €5,000,000 or two-to-four times the value of the illicit benefit. Additional customs, transport, and environmental safety penalties may revoke the special licence required for DG forwarding; criminal prosecution may ensue under Article 301 of the Penal Code for money laundering.

Director personal liability: Directors and compliance officers are criminally liable for AML failures in a DG logistics entity. Conviction may lead to imprisonment, travel bans, seizure of personal and corporate assets, disqualification from board positions, and personal civil liability to compensate third parties harmed by the unlawful shipments.
